### [Weave: Routing-Adaptive Warp Scheduling for MoE Megakernels](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27765>)

Weave chooses spatial warp allocations and phase-dependent communication roles from each GPU’s routing counts, keeping matrix units active inside a fused mixture-of-experts layer. Its NVIDIA and AMD layer benchmarks show how runtime scheduling can reduce communication and computation imbalance without changing expert routing. Reported layer speedups are substantially larger than the paper’s broader-path latency controls, so they should not be interpreted as whole-request throughput gains.

### [LightningMoBA: Dynamic Routing and KV-Centric Sparse-Attention Execution](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26268>)

LightningMoBA reorganizes sparse prefill around key/value-owned work units, splits high-fanout tasks and overlaps query gathers with GPU matrix work while replacing fixed block budgets with score-relative thresholds. On five checkpoints evaluated with RULER at tensor parallelism eight and batch size one, it reduces generation-loop time by 1.20–1.60× versus FlashMoBA at matched average Top-16 retention, offering a concrete design for turning sparsity into execution savings. Controlled comparisons attribute most Top-16 gains to the execution backend, while dynamic routing becomes more useful at larger budgets; quality still falls on every model at 64K context in the main Top-16 comparison.

## [2026-11-21](../../../reports/2026/11/2026-11-21.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Inkling 2 Mini on vLLM: Per-Pass Caches and Variable-Loop Execution](<https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-11-20-inkling2-mini>)

vLLM’s Inkling2 Mini integration represents repeated core-layer visits as separate cache layers and fuses cross-pass message reads and gated controllers, supporting shared weights without incorrectly sharing each pass’s KV and convolution state. For the separate variable-loop research checkpoint on one GB200 at TP1 and 4K context, reducing three passes to one lowers batch-one forward decode-step time from 3.85 ms to 1.51 ms and raises KV capacity from 175K to 352K tokens; sharing KV across three passes instead yields 194K tokens with similar step time. These controls make loop execution and its memory tradeoffs inspectable, but are rejected by fixed-loop Inkling2 Mini, do not establish a quality–speed frontier and measure forward passes rather than end-to-end serving.

### [SubGPU Pipelining: Intra-GPU Fine-Grained Spatial Parallelism for LLM Inference](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14904>)

SubGPU Pipelining divides a decoding graph into stages on disjoint groups of GPU streaming multiprocessors, then streams microbatches through them to overlap operators with different resource demands. A one-B200 prototype replaying a GPT-OSS 120B deployment shard reduces decoder iteration time by 10.33%, showing how spatial scheduling can improve memory utilization without rewriting the operator kernels. The larger throughput-frontier gains are simulation results, rather than measurements from a 32-GPU serving deployment.

### [Fast by Default: Compile-Time Heuristics for Helion Kernels](<https://pytorch.org/blog/fast-by-default-compile-time-heuristics-for-helion-kernels/>)

This Helion study uses compiler intermediate representation and approximate resource-liveness analysis to choose kernel configurations without running an autotuning search. On the tested H100 reductions, its default configurations reach 1.27 times the speed of vLLM handwritten kernels and approach fully tuned Helion performance, making useful execution speed available before a costly search. The report also shows that heuristic seeds mainly improve the early search, with much smaller benefits near the final best configuration.

## [2026-11-13](../../../reports/2026/11/2026-11-13.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [MegaOps: A Kernel Overlapping Framework with PyTorch-like Modularity and Megakernel Performance](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16248>)

MegaOps overlaps separate GPU kernels by synchronizing on ready tiles of intermediate tensors, preserving operator boundaries while hiding work that would otherwise wait for whole kernels to finish. Its shared data-tiling contract makes it easier to combine compute and communication kernels, with roughly 9–10% higher average decode throughput than the best tested alternatives in offline dense-model experiments. The results concern single-batch forward execution with common sampling and CUDA graphs, rather than online serving latency or universal megakernel superiority.

**Published:** 2026-11-12 · **First seen:** 2026-11-13T11:09:02.287+00:00 · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Kernel Overlap, GPU Runtime, Data-Tile Synchronization

**Public availability:** 2026-11-13T01:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.DC/new>) · [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.DC/recent?skip=0&show=2000>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.16248v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Methods and evaluation in Sections 2–5, plus Appendices A–C, inspected. Data-tile semaphores, kernel-to-data mappings, AsyncStream, dependency-aware prefetching and graph-level tuning allow compatible kernels to overlap without fusing them; closed-source kernels are decomposed into subkernels with proxy synchronization. Dense Llama/Qwen models span 0.6B–70B on single H100/A100/L40 GPUs and 4×A100/8×H100 servers. Authors report five-run medians: average decode throughput 1.10× (single GPU) and 1.09× (multi-GPU) versus the best other tested system, with prefill averages 0.98× and 1.10× respectively. Appendix C.1 extracts vLLM 0.31 forward execution into CUDA graphs and uses the same greedy sampler, intentionally excluding host/framework differences. Original v1 received November 12 at 03:43:34 UTC; its original primary-DC Friday November 13 batch plus the official EST schedule support the inferred November 13 at 01:00 UTC public announcement. No prior covered ID or verified earlier author artifact was found.

**Limitations:** Experiments use fixed batches, selected dense models and one-node GPU systems, not request arrival/SLO or broad accuracy studies. Only one input and one output synchronization tensor are supported per kernel; matching data tilings, correct mappings/targets and peer annotations remain programmer obligations. Deadlock avoidance relies partly on empirically observed CUDA CTA scheduling, and symmetric allocation assumes consistent SPMD execution and coordinated garbage collection. Small-shape reduce-scatter cases fall to 0.62×–0.83× of the best baseline; single-GPU prefill can regress. Graph tuning and source adaptation are required; total tuning amortization and an accessible author code release were not verified. No results independently reproduced.

## [2026-11-10](../../../reports/2026/11/2026-11-10.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Detent: Batch-Invariant LLM Serving and RL Rollouts at Near-Stock Speed](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10611>)

Detent compiles an inference engine’s kernel-selection rules into a dependence graph, fixes a minimal set of batch-dependent values, and tunes those fixed choices for the expected traffic. In the tested deployments, this enables reproducible serving and matching rollout/training probabilities while retaining much of the speed of ordinary vLLM and SGLang.

**Published:** 2026-11-07 · **First seen:** 2026-11-10T11:07:43.741+00:00 · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Deterministic Inference, Kernel Selection, Autotuning, Train-Rollout Consistency

**Public availability:** 2026-11-10T01:00:00Z (inferred from dated announcement and official schedule). [Timing source](<https://arxiv.org/list/cs.LG/new>) · [Timing source](<https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html>)

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2611.10611v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Complete 18-page v1, Sections 3–8 and Appendices A–C inspected. A minimum vertex cut isolates selection from the batch; legal-value checks and per-family tuning commit a fixed tuple. On BF16 Llama-3.1-70B and Qwen3-30B-A3B at TP4 on four H100s, geometric-mean median latency per output token is 1.08–1.11x the same engine’s Stock across the tested workloads, with three runs per cell; all applicable batch-invariance cells pass. Seeded rollouts replay and rescore exactly in the tested 512-sample batteries, while the separate 8B trainer experiment matches same-weight token probabilities. New contribution is automated selection analysis and tuning, beyond previously covered bitwise-alignment recipes. Original primary cs.LG November10 batch plus the official EST schedule imply November10 01:00 UTC public availability, not the November7 receipt time.

**Limitations:** Invariance assumes batch-invariant kernels and request-local mathematics and holds only for a fixed model, deployment, engine build and commitment tuple. Users must transcribe selectors; legality may be sampled offline but is checked at runtime. Traffic drift can make an old tuple much slower; dynamic batch-wide FP8 scales are outside scope. Large deterministic-mode gaps partly include overloaded queues, and RL stability tests do not establish universal prevention of collapse or correction of stale weights. No author implementation or independent reproduction was verified.

### [One Megakernel is Not Enough: Predicting Where to Cut for Streaming Inference](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35336>)

This planner uses conventional execution profiles and implementation contracts to rank where a streaming model should be split into specialized megakernels and how their GPU resources should overlap. Preserving useful boundaries can beat one large kernel: independent scheduling and earlier publication sometimes outweigh the extra launches, while larger batches can favor conventional execution.

It offers a more compact way to optimize decoding kernels while translating some kernel-level improvements into higher serving throughput.

**Published:** 2026-10-02 · **First seen:** 2026-10-03T10:06:42Z · **Novelty:** new · **Tags:** Kernel Autotuning, Quantized Inference, vLLM

[Blog](<https://pytorch.org/blog/building-a-high-performance-and-portable-vllm-linear-backend-with-helion/>) · [Code](<https://github.com/redhat-et/vllm-helion>)

**Evidence:** engineering-report; full-text. The page's publication metadata and official RSS agree on October 2 at 19:55:07 UTC, inside the main interval. The authors report 1.110–1.178x geometric-mean kernel speedups across tested comparisons and over 10% serving-throughput gains for some workloads, using an H100 80GB, dense Qwen models, three 8-bit formats, and ShareGPT. The linked fork includes kernels, configurations, and tuning instructions.

**Limitations:** Helion runs under CUDA Graph replay for at most 32 tokens; larger shapes fall back to existing kernels. Tests disable prefix caching and do not establish cross-hardware portability. The integration is a separate fork, and additional models require offline tuning that can take hours; results were not independently reproduced.

### [MegaFlux: Skew-Resilient MoE Megakernels via Pipelined Expert Replication](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00671>)

MegaFlux dynamically replicates heavily used experts and overlaps replica transfers and gradient reductions with computation inside a mixture-of-experts megakernel. It reduces stragglers caused by uneven routing, making fused expert execution more useful when a few experts attract disproportionate work.

**Published:** 2026-09-30 · **First seen:** 2026-10-02T15:33:57Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** MoE Kernels, Expert Replication, Load Balancing

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00671>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Catch-up discovery: v1 was submitted September 30 at 20:09:09 UTC but is in the October 2 announcement list, consistent with scheduled public release at October 2 00:00 UTC. Eight-B200 experiments include controlled routing sweeps and pipelining ablations; DeepSeek-V4-Pro prefill in vLLM reports 1.13–1.26x median batch-latency speedups over fixed expert placement on 160 LongBench-Pro prompts.

**Limitations:** Layer sweeps use synthetic operands and trace-derived routing distributions, with spare memory for replicas. Small skewed backward workloads can slow down, and tests cover one NVLink domain rather than cross-node deployment. The end-to-end measurement stops at first-token production; no MegaFlux code release was verified.

## [2026-09-30](../../../reports/2026/09/2026-09-30.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [Mixture-of-Kittens: MoE Megakernel for NVL72s](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36070>)

Mixture-of-Kittens fuses expert dispatch, expert computation, and result combination into a deterministic GPU kernel, choosing communication direction per operator and avoiding CPU synchronization. It targets NVL72 systems where conventional mixture-of-experts communication schedules leave performance unused, providing an open implementation for overlapping computation and data movement.

**Published:** 2026-09-28 · **First seen:** 2026-09-30T10:02:58Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** MoE Training, Kernel Fusion, NVL72

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36070>) · [Code](<https://github.com/cursor/mixture-of-kittens>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Newly discovered within the 72-hour catch-up window, absent from the baseline; arXiv v1 was submitted 2026-09-28 at 18:22:34 UTC. Alongside layer benchmarks and ablations, a 512-GB300 comparison changes only the MoE backend and reports 1,070.2 versus 761.0 tokens/second/GPU, a 41% training-throughput increase.

**Limitations:** The full-model result comes from the authors' internal production stack and one reported configuration; the open layer benchmarks use synthetic routing inputs. Gains vary with precision, token count, and expert parallelism, and should not be generalized to other accelerator fabrics or training convergence.

## [2026-09-29 — Landscape baseline](../../../landscape/2026-09-29.md) — PARTIAL SEARCH

### [FlashAttention-4: Algorithm and Kernel Pipelining Co-Design for Asymmetric Hardware Scaling](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05451>)

FlashAttention-4 redesigns attention pipelines for Blackwell GPUs, overlapping matrix operations with softmax while reducing shared-memory traffic and other non-matrix overhead. The CuTe-DSL implementation provides an open example of how attention algorithms and kernels must adapt when compute throughput grows faster than supporting hardware.

**Published:** 2026-03-05 · **First seen:** 2026-09-30T04:13:56.564Z · **Novelty:** baseline · **Tags:** Attention Kernels, Blackwell, CuTe DSL

**Positioning:** frontier-research

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05451>) · [Code](<https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention/tree/main/flash_attn/cute>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. B200 BF16 attention benchmarks span 1K–32K sequences, causal and noncausal masks, and several head dimensions; the authors report up to 1.3x over cuDNN 9.13 and 2.7x over the tested Triton baseline.

**Limitations:** These are attention-kernel measurements, not full-model training speedups. The paper explicitly notes that newer cuDNN releases incorporated similar techniques and achieved comparable performance; gains are hardware- and shape-specific.
